presentingComplaint: High-grade fever with rigors for 5 days, now drowsy with dark urine and reduced urine output, deteriorating despite 2 days of oral chloroquine.
history: Migrant construction worker who returned 12 days ago from a P. falciparum-endemic district of eastern India (Odisha). Five days of intermittent high-grade fever with teeth-chattering rigors followed by drenching sweats, occurring roughly every 36-48 hours, with severe myalgia and anorexia. A local practitioner made a clinical diagnosis of malaria and started oral chloroquine 48 hours ago; instead of improving he has become progressively more unwell with persisting daily fevers, passing dark 'cola-coloured' urine, and today the family report him being confused and difficult to rouse. No prior antimalarials in this region are reliably effective as chloroquine-resistant falciparum is well established locally. No cough, dysuria, diarrhoea, neck stiffness or rash. No prior splenectomy. Not on regular medication; no known G6PD status.
examination: Ill-looking, drowsy but rousable, icteric sclerae. Mildly dehydrated. Pallor present. Chest clear; abdomen soft with a palpable spleen 3 cm below costal margin and mild tender hepatomegaly. No focal neurological deficit, no meningism, no rash or eschar. Capillary refill 3 seconds, cool peripheries.

labs.parasitaemia: P. falciparum ring forms, 6% parasitised RBCs

imaging: USG abdomen: mild hepatosplenomegaly, no biliary dilatation, no focal hepatic lesion, no ascites. Chest X-ray clear.
microbiology: Peripheral thick and thin smear: Plasmodium falciparum, only ring-stage trophozoites and occasional banana-shaped gametocytes seen, parasite density ~6% (approx 300,000/µL) — high parasitaemia. Rapid diagnostic test positive for P. falciparum HRP-2 antigen, negative for pan-Plasmodium/P. vivax LDH. Blood cultures sterile at 48h. This represents chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum with clinical progression on chloroquine, meeting WHO criteria for severe malaria (hyperparasitaemia, jaundice, AKI, impaired consciousness, hypoglycaemia).
finalDiagnosis: Severe chloroquine-resistant Plasmodium falciparum malaria with cerebral involvement, acute kidney injury, jaundice and hypoglycaemia — requiring escalation from failed oral chloroquine to parenteral artesunate.
citations: WHO — Guidelines for Malaria (severe malaria, parenteral artesunate) — 2023
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Malaria
NVBDCP/ICMR India — National Guidelines for Diagnosis and Treatment of Malaria — 2014
stewardship: This is a treatment-failure/resistance scenario: chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum with clinical deterioration on oral chloroquine, now meeting severe-malaria criteria (impaired consciousness, parasitaemia >5%, AKI, jaundice, hypoglycaemia, lactate >2). Escalate immediately to IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24h then daily; this is superior to quinine (SEAQUAMAT/AQUAMAT). Continue parenteral therapy for a minimum of 24h and until able to tolerate orals, then complete a full 3-day course of oral artemisinin-based combination therapy (artemether-lumefantrine) to prevent recrudescence; add primaquine single 0.25 mg/kg gametocytocidal dose after G6PD screening. 'Source control' here is parasite clearance plus supportive ICU care: correct hypoglycaemia, judicious fluids, monitor for haemolysis and delayed post-artesunate haemolytic anaemia. Antibacterials are not routinely indicated but empirical cover is warranted only if concurrent bacterial sepsis is suspected.
contraindications: Chloroquine is inappropriate/ineffective for chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum — do not continue.
Avoid mefloquine as a partner in cerebral malaria due to neuropsychiatric risk.
Check G6PD status before primaquine to avoid acute haemolysis.
Avoid aggressive fluid boluses (FEAST) — risk of pulmonary oedema in severe malaria.
edgeCases: Delayed post-artesunate haemolytic anaemia at day 7-21 requires Hb monitoring after discharge.
Hypoglycaemia may be masked by quinine-induced hyperinsulinaemia if quinine is used.
Coma may be attributed to hypoglycaemia rather than cerebral malaria — recheck glucose.
High parasitaemia with only ring forms can under-represent sequestered burden.
expectedMaiK: Severe falciparum malaria failing oral chloroquine (chloroquine-resistant) mandates immediate escalation to IV artesunate plus supportive care, not another oral agent.
expectedNextQuestions: Exact travel dates and specific endemic region visited?
What antimalarial, dose and duration has already been given?
Any reduction in urine output or dark urine (blackwater)?
G6PD status and prior haemolysis history?
expectedInvestigations: Urgent thick and thin peripheral smear with parasite density (% parasitaemia)
FBC, renal function, LFTs, lactate, coagulation
Blood cultures to exclude concurrent bacteraemia

investigations: Peripheral blood smear (thick and thin) with parasite density

regressionAssertions: Must identify severe/complicated falciparum malaria and escalate to IV artesunate.
Must NOT continue or recommend chloroquine given chloroquine resistance and clinical failure.
Must recognise severe-malaria criteria (impaired consciousness, hyperparasitaemia, AKI, jaundice, hypoglycaemia).
Must include follow-on oral ACT to complete treatment and prevent recrudescence.
